transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-06 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~41m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Tom (CTO - Catalyst Quant), Priya (MLOps), Ramesh (Finance)

Auto Summary: quick discovery focused on cost per token, how batching and caching reduce unit cost, and whether hosted or dedicated is the right fit given budget and latency SLOs.

[00:00:05] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, um, thanks for joining, really quick intros - I'm Jordan, I run the AE for this region, and with me is Maya, our SE.
[00:00:14] Maya (SE): hi all, hi, hello, excited to dig in.
[00:00:18] Tom (CTO): Hey, Tom here, thanks. We, uh, want to understand cost tradeoffs, like per-token economics vs reserved capacity.
[00:00:26] Priya (MLOps): Priya here, I'll be owning the pilot and ops side, mostly interested in latency and whether we can meet our 100ms tail SLOs.
[00:00:33] Ramesh (Finance): Ramesh from finance, hi. Our annual budget for inference is roughly $700k - $1M depending on pilot outcomes.

[00:01:02] Jordan: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: 1) current stack and traffic profile, 2) unit cost drivers and levers (batching/caching/quantization), 3) hosted vs dedicated vs private, 4) next steps. Sound good?
[00:01:10] Tom: Yep.

[00:02:05] Tom: Right now we're running a mixture - a few models on OpenAI for baseline, but majority of heavy inference is in-house on a GPU cluster, cost is kinda high and ops overhead is crazy. We do synchronous low-latency RAG queries and some async batch scoring.
[00:02:25] Priya: Our peak qps is about 120 requests/sec, average tokens per request ~800, but we have a long tail with 4k context calls 10% of the time.
[00:02:40] Maya: ok that's helpful. So two profiles: a steady low-latency stream and an occasional large context workload. Are you instrumenting token breakdowns today?
[00:02:49] Tom: Not in depth, we mostly estimate.

[00:03:30] Jordan: For cost econ, two levers matter most: per-token unit price (hosted) vs amortized GPU $/hr in dedicated, and workload optimizations - batching, prefix/KV caching, and quantization. We'll walk through examples.
[00:03:45] Ramesh: Can you give ballpark numbers? Like, when is dedicated cheaper?

[00:04:10] Maya: Sure. Very coarse: hosted per-token might be $0.0006 - $0.0025 per token depending on model and tier; dedicated TCO depends on committed capacity - e.g., a reserved A100-equivalent fleet amortized could get you effective per-token costs lower for sustained high throughput but you pay fixed commit. The crossover depends on utilization.
[00:04:34] Tom: that hosted per-token spread is big. What about caching?

[00:05:00] Maya: caching (prefix/KV) can reduce tokens served by de-duplicating repeated contexts - in our experience 10-40% token reduction for many RAG flows. Batching reduces per-token overhead by fusing attention work, especially for short sequences; can get 20-60% improvements depending on latency SLOs. But batching introduces a latency tradeoff.
[00:05:22] Priya: For our sync path, tail latency is critical - can't afford extra 50ms for batching. Is there smart batching?

[00:05:35] Maya: yes, we do continuous batching with latency caps; you configure a max-wait (e.g., 10ms) and Redwood dynamically groups requests. Also we do priority lanes so interactive requests can bypass larger batch windows.
[00:05:48] Tom: does that require changing client code?
[00:05:52] Maya: no, it's runtime-level. You can set policies per route.

[00:06:20] Jordan: On dedicated vs hosted: hosted is fastest time-to-value and no infra to run; dedicated gives predictable unit costs at scale and isolation; private (VPC/on-prem) is for compliance - higher ops. For your budget, we can model both.
[00:06:40] Ramesh: Our budget needs predictability, not surprises. If we commit to dedicated, what's the minimum term?
[00:06:47] Jordan: Typically monthly reserved pools with 6-12 month contracts for committed discounts. We also do burst capacity for traffic spikes.

[00:07:30] Tom: What about model variants and quantization? We run some models with FP16 / int8.
[00:07:36] Maya: quantization to int8 or int4 can reduce memory and throughput costs a lot. Redwood supports quantized variants and will route to the best kernel; quality impact depends on model and evals. We can recommend quantization profiles per model.
[00:07:55] Tom: Great. How do you handle fallback if quantized model has a regression?
[00:08:00] Maya: We do canary rollouts and automatic fallback to a more precise variant when quality degrades beyond thresholds - integrated into rollout policies.

[00:08:40] Priya: Security wise, if we go dedicated but hosted, do you do VPC peering or private networking?
[00:08:48] Jordan: For Dedicated we offer a private network plane and customer data isolation; Private deployments give customer-managed control plane with KMS integrations.
[00:08:58] Ramesh: SOC 2?
[00:09:01] Jordan: SOC 2 Type II, ISO in progress, SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs - we can share the pack.

[00:10:30] Tom: Back to numbers: let's say we have 120 qps peak, avg 800 tokens, 10% 4k context. How do you model that?
[00:10:39] Maya: We'll take your qps x token distribution, simulate expected batching efficiency - short sequences batch better - and then estimate per-token time on target hardware. For example, with a 1k-seq model on a GPU optimized runtime you might see X tokens/sec; we multiply that by costs. We'll run a quick calc and share.
[00:11:05] Jordan: To ground this: if you used hosted medium-tier model at $0.0009/token, and average tokens per request 800 with 120 qps sustained for an hour, cost/hour = 120 * 800 * $0.0009 = ~ $86.4/hr => ~ $630k/yr. If we can get batching and caching to reduce tokens by 30% that's ~ $440k/yr. If dedicated amortized drops unit cost by 40% vs hosted, might be even lower but you pay reserved fees.
[00:12:02] Ramesh: Ok that's in our range, but the reserved commitment we need to justify. Do you have a TCO model?

[00:12:20] Jordan: yes, Maya will produce a TCO spreadsheet comparing hosted pay-as-you-go, dedicated reserved at different utilization bands, and private on-prem estimates. We'll include sensitivity to caching and batching.

[00:13:05] Priya: For our 4k context calls, latency jumps - do you shard long-context to separate pool?
[00:13:11] Maya: yes recommended pattern: route long context to a larger-memory pool (or an optimized kernel) and keep interactive short context requests on low-latency instances. Smart routing helps avoid noisy neighbor.

[00:13:40] Tom: What about GPU types? A100 vs H100 vs L40?
[00:13:46] Maya: we benchmark across common GPUs; H100 gives better throughput for some models but cost-per-hour is higher. We pick kernels accordingly; our runtime compiles for best choice. We'll include model-specific perf numbers in the follow-up.

[00:14:30] Jordan: Question from finance - how do you show actual token usage so there's no surprise?
[00:14:36] Maya: Redwood Console gives token-level cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and can export token logs (redacted) for cost auditing. Also can set hard quotas.

[00:15:10] Ramesh: Will that include cached hit/miss metrics?
[00:15:13] Maya: yes cache hit rate is tracked and attributed to routes.

[00:15:50] Tom: On the hosted pricing tiers, are there volume discounts?
[00:15:55] Jordan: yes, we tier pricing and also offer committed discounts for Dedicated. We'll map your usage and show breakpoint pricing.

[00:16:30] Priya: Any required client-side changes for caching?
[00:16:33] Maya: no, prefix/KV caching is handled at runtime; you can mark segments as cacheable. Sometimes you want deterministic caching keys - that's a small code change.

[00:17:20] Tom: We're concerned about hallucination/regression if we quantize; how do you validate quality?
[00:17:26] Maya: Redwood Optimize ties model changes to evals and prompt suites - you define golden prompts and we run regression alerts. For pilot we'd run a small eval set.

[00:18:10] Ramesh: Ok, can you give example numbers where batching reduces cost?

[00:18:17] Maya: Example: 1k-seq average, without batching you get say 50k tokens/sec on a GPU; with batching you might hit 80k tokens/sec because overhead amortizes. So cost-per-token drops accordingly. Exact numbers depend on model and token distribution.

[00:19:05] Jordan: Also consider autoscaling and burst capacity; if you need headroom for spikes, hosted can be simpler but costlier. Dedicated with burst or hybrid routing often gives best cost predictability.

[00:19:38] Tom: Hybrid routing meaning some requests go to hosted fallback?
[00:19:41] Maya: yes, you can set policy: primary dedicated, fallback to hosted during saturation. That keeps apps online.

[00:20:10] Priya: For the pilot, how long and what's success?
[00:20:14] Jordan: Typical pilot 4-6 weeks: integrate SDK, run traffic capture/benchmarks, measure cost and latency, then decide on dedicated commit. Success criteria: meet latency SLOs 95th percentile and show unit cost below target and acceptable quality.

[00:20:40] Tom: Sounds good. On billing, do you export usage to our finance system?
[00:20:45] Jordan: We can provide usage exports and invoices with line items per route/model.

[00:21:30] Ramesh: For the committed model, is there a true-up?
[00:21:33] Jordan: yes we do monthly true-ups and adjustable burst policies.

[00:22:05] Tom: Any gotchas we should know?
[00:22:08] Maya: watch out for long-tail tokens (4k+) - they can skew costs quickly; also embeddings workloads have different cost dynamics. Compression of prompts and placement of retrieval can cut tokens significantly.

[00:22:40] Priya: We'll need an initial run of your cost sheet with our numbers.
[00:22:44] Jordan: we'll do that.

[00:23:10] Maya: a quick note on engineering effort: Dedicated setup usually takes a couple weeks for capacity provisioning and network, Private/VPC might be longer with customer network setup. Hosted is immediate.

[00:23:40] Tom: Ok, let's talk about sample numbers. We'll give you our traffic profile.
[00:23:44] Priya: I'll share logs and top prompts.

[00:24:20] Jordan: great - if you can also share current cost numbers for in-house GPU ops that helps the TCO.

[00:24:44] Ramesh: We will. Also want to flag procurement: we may need standard MSAs and security questionnaires.

[00:24:51] Jordan: noted, we'll include security docs and an SOW template.

[00:25:30] Tom: A couple more technical Qs: how do you measure effective batch size and does continuous batching hurt tail p50/p95?
[00:25:37] Maya: we measure both batch size and wait time; p50 often improves with batching, p95 depends on policy - with low max-wait and priority lanes you can keep p95 close to no-batch. We'll show example curves.

[00:26:20] Tom: For caching, do you evict by LRU and are hits per-route?
[00:26:24] Maya: yes LRU plus configurable TTLs and per-route attribution. Sometimes cache keys are tricky for RAG so we'll help with key design.

[00:27:00] Priya: What's support like during pilot?
[00:27:03] Jordan: SE support during pilot, weekly check-ins, and an onboarding guide.

[00:27:30] Tom: Any startup-like discounts?
[00:27:33] Jordan: we can discuss pilot pricing credits and favorable initial committed terms; we'll include options in the pricing sheet.

[00:28:10] Ramesh: Ok good. Are there examples of customers who moved from OpenAI to Redwood and saved money?
[00:28:15] Maya: yes, we have case studies - one quant firm reduced per-token cost by ~35% through batching and dedicated commit. We'll share a redacted case study.

[00:29:00] Tom: About quality again - you mentioned Redwood Optimize ties regressions to prompt sets, can that be automated?
[00:29:06] Maya: yes you can set continuous evals and alerts on drift.

[00:29:40] Jordan: Ok, quick recap and next steps: we'll take the traffic profile (Priya), run the cost model (Maya), share pricing and TCO (Jordan), and schedule a follow-up demo if the numbers look good.
[00:29:55] Priya: I'll get logs to you by Monday (2026-03-09).
[00:30:02] Ramesh: we'll need the security pack too.

[00:31:10] Maya: a couple small clarifications while I have you - what's your expected sustained utilization percentage of peak?
[00:31:16] Tom: probably around 60% sustained during market hours, lower nights.
[00:31:22] Maya: ok that helps.

[00:32:00] Jordan: Any other blockers?
[00:32:02] Tom: none on tech, procurement will review docs.

[00:33:15] Jordan: Great. We'll send the items and propose a follow-up on 2026-03-12.
[00:33:22] Tom: Works.

[00:34:00] -- brief chatter/hold music --
[00:36:10] Priya: small Q - do you support mixed-precision kernels per-seq?
[00:36:14] Maya: runtime supports mixed kernels and dynamic quantization selection per model.

[00:37:50] Tom: thanks everyone. Last ask - can you show model variant perf for our top-2 models?
[00:37:56] Maya: yes we'll include in the follow-up.

[00:39:10] Jordan: ok thanks all, we'll follow up with spreadsheet and security docs.
[00:39:18] Ramesh: thanks.
[00:39:23] Tom: thanks, bye.

[00:41:12] Meeting end.
